about: The words laid under a Renaissance piece's notes (public/shared/conducting/underlay.js; research/RENAISSANCE_COUNTERPOINT_PLAN.md, "Words" and "The words at the phrase's end, and between rests"): each rule of the period's underlay a cost, `whole` where none is broken that another choice keeps, each at Palestrina's own rate once a texted corpus of his measures how often he breaks it.

underlay.about: Each voice's words, from its entry in a point to its entry in the next, laid on its notes by one pass of dynamic programming over each stretch between rests, the cheapest placement under these costs: Jeppesen's nine rules of underlay (pp. 159-160), "as they were formulated in the sixteenth century by Vicentino and Zarlino, and as they were observed by the composers of Palestrina's day", the cadence's syllable and the words' units, and what is ours until measured.

whole.reason: a whole rule's cost: broken only where nothing else is possible, no preference below reaching it -- what `whole` stands for in every setting below

short.reason: a syllable on a note shorter than half the beat (Jeppesen's rule 3: "a note value which is less than a quarter cannot bear a syllable")

crotchet.reason: a syllable on a note shorter than the beat but for rule 2's crotchet (rules 1 and 2), a repeated pitch (9) taking its syllable all the same. 500 since 16 November 2026 (200 before): over the cadence's rule (7, `goal`) with its `final` together, under 9's whole rule

afterShort.reason: a syllable begun after a note shorter than the beat (rule 6: "it is not good to change syllables of the text after note values less than the half note")

afterShortAtEnd.reason: the same on a phrase's last note: the cadence's licence (rule 7: "out of regard for this one will often tolerate" 6 broken, "especially in the cadences")

afterDotted.reason: a syllable begun after a dotted beat, but for rule 2's crotchet (rule 6: "preferably one should not shift syllables after dotted half notes")

repeated.reason: a strong preference, not a whole rule, since 16 November 2026, late: at 300, with the fitted melisma costs, a repeated pitch takes a new syllable 92.0 times in a hundred on the composer's prima partes (research/renaissance-mass/melisma-fit.mjs --repeated: the same from 100 to 400), the nearest it comes to his 89.4; the voice re-articulates a repeated pitch it holds (soloist.mjs, voices/singing.json `reArticulation`; the owner: "re-articulating repeated notes inside melismas ... you're also clear to pursue building these"). his fully worded parts give a repeated pitch a new syllable 89.4 times in a hundred (his Kyries, Sanctus and Agnus Dei 76.6; CPDL's editions, research/renaissance-mass/stress-accord.mjs --worded 0.95, 16 November 2026), so a whole rule was a little purer than he is. a repeated pitch held on a syllable, but after an anticipation (rule 9: "repetition of tones requires new syllables of the text, with the exception of tonal entries that have ornamental character")

final.reason: a phrase's last syllable not begun on its last note (rule 7: "it is natural that the final syllable should coincide with the final tone in the musical phrase")

midWord.reason: a phrase never ended within a word, as Palestrina's generation's rules have it: a rest an ending "in the procedure of speech" (Vicentino 1555, his rule 9: harran-1973-vicentino). Josquin's generation let a rest fall within a word and meant nothing by it: the earliest writing on underlay (Venice, Marciana Lat. 336, c. 1440, in king-1999's translation as drake-2006 reads it; harran-1978-origins) gives the words' placing to "the understanding of whoever has to place them", and its examples break "Chi-ri-e" with a rest; drake-2006 finds that composers c. 1500 "were not operating with an unwritten theory about word-tone relations". The period's texted Kyries (jrp-scores, their underlay their modern editors') end 87 of their 1,781 phrases between rests within a word, 4.9 in a hundred -- some thirty the encodings' own hyphens, the rest within "eleison", Josquin's 28 -- so that a profile for that generation would let a broken word through at some 3 in a hundred: not asked (research/RENAISSANCE_COUNTERPOINT_PLAN.md, "Mid-word endings in the period"; research/renaissance-mass/kyrie-phrases-jrp.mjs)

goal.reason: a voice still singing its point's phrase at the point's cadence without the phrase's last syllable sounding on the goal's note, that syllable begun before the goal's note costing `final` (rule 7 at the cadence; the owner, 16 November 2026: "make sure the parts end on the same syllable in each phrase, with no part partway through a word"). Over every preference, under the whole rules -- a syllable on a crotchet among them, which 7 does not license: on the composer's sections the voices on the phrase's last syllable at a goal 58.1 to 85.9 in a hundred, within a word 25.8 to 4.5, the Kyries' 93.7 and 5.4, where the period's texted Kyries end a section's every voice on "-son" 87 times in a hundred (jrp-scores; research/renaissance-mass/phrases-and-words.mjs, kyrie-phrases-jrp.mjs)

imitation.reason: a note of a later entry's statement not laid as the first entry's (rule 8: "in imitation, the setting of the text at the first appearance of the theme must be maintained without change in all subsequent entries")

stress.reason: an accented syllable on a note less prominent than a minim on a beat (rule 5, "so far as practicable"): ours, until a texted corpus of Palestrina's measures how he places them

stressPair.reason: within a word, an accented syllable on a note less prominent than one beside it (rule 5): ours, until measured

holdStressed.reason: each note an accented syllable is held over (a melisma's place): fitted on 16 November 2026 to Palestrina's practice as 27 CPDL editions of his masses give it (cpdl-palestrina-masses: 8,008 words of two or more syllables; their underlay their editors'): a new syllable on 61.8 of a hundred notes in his fully worded parts (50.7 in his Kyries, Sanctus and Agnus Dei), and of melismas of three notes or more 58.1 in a hundred on the word's stress and 29.3 on its unstressed last syllable. (Corrected the same night: the fit was first aimed at 30.5 of a hundred notes, CPDL's files leaving half their parts' notes without words; on the 70 fully worded parts, research/renaissance-mass/stress-accord.mjs --worded 0.95. Searched again against the corrected rates, within his rules 7 and 8: these costs 0.028 from his rates, the nearest 0.025 -- holdStressed and holdUnstressed 0.2, repeat 1: a new syllable on 63.5 of a hundred notes, melismas 43.0 on the stress and 33.8 on a last syllable -- the two alike, these kept.) Searched with `holdUnstressed` and `repeat` on 24 of the composer's prima partes (the selection's voicings, seeds 1 to 6; research/renaissance-mass/melisma-fit.mjs), the planner's notes fixed, no further than the period's whole rules allow: past a `repeat` of 3 the underlay begins to break Jeppesen's rule 8 (an entry's statement set as the first entry's: 82 of 93 entries at 10, the test's floor 90 in a hundred) and rule 7 (the phrase's last syllable on its last note: 20 in 3,436 notes at 300), which Palestrina keeps. Before, a new syllable on 61.2 of a hundred notes, melismas 83.2 on the stress and 7.9 on a last syllable; now 55.5, 67.7 and 17.1 -- toward his on each, the rest of the excess the planner's subjects, about a note a syllable, which no cost of the underlay's reaches (at 300, 48.9, 58.6 and 23.3, the rules broken) (the owner, 16 November 2026: "placement of syllables and accord between the melodic lines and stress of the syllables, to the extent that Palestrina does likewise"; "the planner likely needs to receive the text to inform the planning process")

longAfter.reason: a melisma's length past which each note it is held over costs `longEach`: ours, until measured

longEach.reason: each note a syllable is held over past `longAfter`: ours, until measured

repeat.reason: the phrase begun again, at any of its words, once a word is done: fitted on 16 November 2026 to Palestrina's practice as 27 CPDL editions of his masses give it (cpdl-palestrina-masses: 8,008 words of two or more syllables; their underlay their editors'): a new syllable on 61.8 of a hundred notes in his fully worded parts (50.7 in his Kyries, Sanctus and Agnus Dei), and of melismas of three notes or more 58.1 in a hundred on the word's stress and 29.3 on its unstressed last syllable. startAtPause.reason: a stretch between rests begun past its phrase's first word, after a comma, colon or full stop -- at a unit of the words' bounds (the owner, 16 November 2026: "each phrase (anything bounded by rests) should generally match a complete phrase in the lyrics"): ours

startWithin.reason: a stretch begun after another word, within a unit of the words: ours. The period's texted Kyries sing whole units between their rests 80.5 times in a hundred of 1,781 (jrp-scores), the composer's Kyries 99.4 at any cost from 1.5 to a whole rule's -- their units short -- and its motets' units a comma's whole clause of up to fourteen syllables, broken where their sense breaks within it, which no comma marks; Palestrina's own rate waits on his texted music (research/SOURCES_TO_FETCH.md)

cutAtPause.reason: a stretch ended before its phrase's last word, at a comma, colon or full stop: ours

cut.reason: a stretch ended at another word's end, within a unit of the words: ours, as `startWithin`

gap.unit: cost (a whole rule's the `whole`) for each word left unsung
gap.reason: a voice leaves none of its phrase's words unsung: a stretch after a rest begins where its words go on, or back at a word it has sung (its phrase again, at `repeat`), never past one it has not; its last stretch in the phrase ends on the phrase's last syllable, each word it would leave this cost -- finite, so that where its notes cannot hold the words a placement is still found, and counted (the owner, 16 November 2026: "also fix the problem you identified with gaps in text", of the selection's duo, its Cantus singing "Cum ... Cum, dies Pentecostes" and never "complerentur": each stretch had been laid by itself, free to begin at any word). A word ended within counts among the words left, and a stretch after a rest begins at a word's start, so that a word is never sung half: the owner, the same night, "The scores should really not be either leaving out words out (unless Palestrina allows this) OR half-singing them, but yes, half-sung is worse than left out" -- of O magnum mysterium's Tenor, which had ended a stretch on "na-" where a word left out cost the same
